items.title: Used-Car Prices Soar: $30,000 Buys a Toyota With 90,000 Miles
body: Benjamin Young’s recent wrangling on the used-car lot shows just how punishing America’s affordability crisis has become.

The Florida resident paid $30,000 for a Toyota 4Runner loaded with the features he wanted — but the SUV has been driven 90,000 miles and is 12 years old. In 2023, he bought a Toyota Venza with similar mileage for half that price.
“I’m definitely getting less for the money,” said Young, a 48-year-old process engineer near Jacksonville.

So are the millions shopping the pre-owned lots these days. A used car priced between $10,000 and $15,000 today is almost nine years old on average and has 98,000 miles on it, according to auto research site Edmunds. In 2019, the same budget bought a car under five years old with about 58,000 miles.

The squeeze starts with new cars, which are selling for record prices and eventually command hefty premiums when they hit the used market. A new 4Runner now costs about twice what Young paid, while even a basic Honda Civic starts at $25,000. For buyers on tighter budgets, that increasingly means settling for older, higher-mileage vehicles that are more likely to need repairs.

It’s the latest sign of how the traditional American dream is increasingly tougher to attain. Voters returned President Donald Trump to the White House partly on his vow to bring prices down. But inflation has been back above 3% — the level when Trump took office — since the president went to war with Iran in late February, sending energy prices soaring.

US mortgage rates last week climbed to the highest level in more than a year, and consumer sentiment slid below estimates in September. Polls show Democrats are leading in their bid to retake the House of Representatives in the November midterm elections and have a good shot at control of the Senate with Trump’s approval ratings lagging.

This week, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates, and investors are betting more hikes are in store to cool inflation. That’s going to make borrowing even more expensive for Americans already grappling with a structural change in the car market.

For two decades leading up to the Covid-19 pandemic, new models were affordable and more buyers were leasing. Competitive automakers pushed big rebates, cheap leases and 0% financing to ramp up sales. Those leases sent a parade of low-mileage cars to the used lots every year.
Problems with the supply chain during the pandemic hurt sales, but they taught auto companies a lesson: Producing fewer, high-priced models means better profits and rewards from stock investors.

After years of static share movement, General Motors Co. and Ford Motor Co. both have gotten investor attention in part with price-backed profit strength and raised earnings guidance this year. In its second-quarter earnings release, GM boasted about its average vehicle sale price of $52,000 and sales incentives that are below most competitors. Ford had similar results, saying net pricing helped lift its quarterly profit by $200 million.

GM is selling new versions of its Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra pickups later this year. Since buyers pay more for redesigned models, GM Chief Financial Officer Paul Jacobson told investors at a Morgan Stanley investor event this month that “means there is pricing potential.”

While that may sound like “greedflation” — favoring big margins over winning new buyers — some of it is necessity, said Diane Swonk, KPMG’s chief economist. Trump’s tariffs have cost automakers billions of dollars, and the war with Iran has increased energy costs, especially for diesel fuel that truckers need to ship parts and vehicles around North America.

The average new car now sells for $50,000. With cars losing around 40% of their value after three years, the average used vehicle sells for more than $30,000. In 2019, the sales price was about $20,000, says Edmunds.

Those inflated prices eventually land in the used-car market, which is getting lower inventories because of a drop in leases. Before Covid, Americans leased about 4 million vehicles a year, most of which sold as used after three or four years. This year, the industry is on pace to lease 2.5 million, which could tighten the used market for the foreseeable future, said Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds.
He said automakers aren’t offering low-interest lease deals like they used to because the incentives are too expensive in the current interest-rate environment and so they prefer to sell vehicles.
“We just don’t have the churn,” said Swonk, the economist.
Used cars selling for less than $20,000 are tougher to find and have high mileage, and dealers have to fight to get them, said Rhett Ricart, who owns multiple dealerships in Columbus, Ohio.
“They’re like gold,” Ricart said. “They’re out there, but we have to pay record prices to get them.”
Competition is fierce for buyers, too.

It took Amy Hyken of Kansas months of scrolling through websites to find a used Lexus NX 250 under 50,000 miles going for $35,000. But it was in Florida — she had to spend $800 and wait another two months to have it shipped to her home near Kansas City. She did manage to claw back the shipping fee since the delivery was delayed.
“It’s a thinner market than it was in the past,” said Hyken, 58, a child family therapist. “I’m paying more, and finding the car I want is harder.”

Then there’s the risk that cars with high mileage will need repairs shortly after purchase. While Young said he loves his 4Runner, he’s dealing with a fluid leak affecting the shocks. Shops are quoting him prices in the thousands to fix the problem, and Young’s been bickering with his retailer to pay for it.
“It’s kind of the way of the world,” he said.

items.title: Mozambique Cut by Moody's on Heightened Restructuring Risks
body: Moody’s Ratings cut its assessment of Mozambique’s creditworthiness deeper into junk, citing increased risk that the gas-rich southeast African nation will restructure its sole eurobond.
The rating was cut by a notch to Caa3, the company said in a statement late Friday.

“The downgrade reflects higher risks that the government restructures private-sector foreign-currency debt, including the eurobond,” Moody’s said. “Financing and payment pressures previously concentrated in the domestic debt market have spread to external debt.”

Mozambique has faced intense fiscal pressures over the past two years, as post-election violence battered an already struggling economy. That’s amplified debt-servicing difficulties, and Moody’s said external arrears had by the end of last year increased to $328 million, equivalent to 1.3% of gross domestic product.
Read more: Senegal, Mozambique Debt Beats EM Peers on IMF Talk Progress

While the government has so far stayed current on payments for its $900 million eurobond due 2031, the Caa3 rating is consistent with a debt restructuring that would constitute a default and result in investor losses of 20% to 35%, the ratings company said.

Mozambique has been in talks with the International Monetary Fund for a fresh bailout, and the Washington-based lender’s mission ended on Friday. Economic activity remains subdued but it’s showing signs of recovery, the fund said. The government said the next visit could be in November, and lead to a staff-level agreement on a deal.
The Moody’s downgrade could come as a surprise to investors, who’ve pushed the price of Mozambique’s dollar notes up by nearly 30% from their April lows to 94.88 cents, the highest since March 2020.

Companies led by TotalEnergies SE have been forging ahead with a $20 billion liquefied natural gas export project that could transform the economy of one of the world’s poorest nations. Another Exxon Mobil Corp.-led group is set to approve another even bigger adjacent facility by year-end.

items.title: Great Lakes Bind US, Canada Trade Imperiled by Trump Tariffs
body: The American Century often draws a crowd when the ship pulls into the Port of Duluth-Superior to load Minnesota iron ore. Kids cheer when the captain blasts the fog horn. A voice on the loudspeaker retells the story of how the 1,000-foot-long bulk carrier has sailed the Great Lakes for nearly a half century.

It’s a momentary flashback to the waning days of US industrial primacy. The vessel was built in 1981 in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin, and runs on four General Motors Co. diesel engines that generate more horsepower than a dozen Formula 1 cars. It set records for coal payloads in the 1990s. The current owner is American Steamship Co., a unit of Mainstay Maritime that’s based in Williamsville, New York, and was founded in Buffalo in 1907.

But for all the Made-in-America pride, aging “lakers” like American Century have depended on a regional economy that moved in lockstep with Canada. Coal volumes have hit hard times, and US tariffs have disrupted trade in iron ore. Adding to the uncertainty now is a rift between Ottawa and Washington that threatens lasting damage to supply chains across land and water geared for free-flowing commerce.

“Hope isn’t a strategy, but we would expect that this trade war comes to an end at some point and we can get back to regular business,” said Kevin Beardsley, executive director of the Duluth Seaway Port Authority, located less than 200 miles from the Canadian border. “Canada is looking at different supply chains and that type of thing, and that is a risk the longer this goes on.”

President Donald Trump has offered mixed messages recently, saying in Ireland last weekend that there may be a deal with Canada “fairly soon” but issued fresh threats when asked this week about Ottawa’s overtures to the European Union. Prime Minister Mark Carney told Bloomberg News on Monday that Canada is “ready to sit down” for talks.
Read More: Carney Says US Deal Possible, Blow-Up Helped Clarify ‘Red Lines’
That would come as welcome relief to those who depend on waterborne cargo between by both countries.

Through August, vessel traffic at Duluth-Superior was down 23% from a year earlier, according to data provided by the port. Visits by US-flagged ships fell about 19% and arrivals by Canadian carriers sank 37%. Coal volumes totaled 4.7 million tons in 2025 and are on track to reach just 500,000 tons this year, the lowest level since 1973.

While the overall drop is blamed mostly on the closure of a coal terminal, there’s also less northbound tonnage of iron ore, the steel-making feedstock mined near Duluth in the US’s richest iron ranges, hauled across the lakes and delivered these days mostly to mills in Ohio or Indiana. Trump’s tariffs on the metal have done significant damage to Canada’s steel sector.
Domestic iron ore shipments from Duluth-Superior are running 40% below the 2025 pace.

The biggest of the Great Lakes ports by tonnage, Duluth-Superior sits on the western edge of a 2,300-mile (3,700-kilometer) trade route that includes the St. Lawrence Seaway, all connected by locks. The maritime borders between the countries extend across Lake Superior, Huron, Erie and Ontario, and a stretch of the St. Lawrence River that eventually spills into a gulf near the Atlantic Ocean north of Nova Scotia.

With about two-fifths of the US-Canada border going across water, 200 million tons of cargo — bulk commodities including coal, grain, iron ore, limestone, salt, sand and stone — move annually on the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence. By comparison, American railroads haul about 1.5 billion tons of raw materials and finished goods a year.

“Over decades and decades of time, the Great Lakes, the states and the provinces have become a hugely integrated – the third-largest economy in the world if it was a country,” with $6 trillion in economic activity across the region, said Ian Hamilton, president and CEO of the Hamilton-Oshawa Port Authority, or HOPA, a marine port network on Lake Ontario near Toronto.

Lately his US counterparts are “all kind of scratching their heads going, ‘Why are we disrupting this integrated market?’” Hamilton said of the recent volley of tariffs. “We’ve crossed the borders to drink in each other’s bars and eat other’s food and vacation at each other’s properties.”

Among the strategies to diversify its dependence away from the US, HOPA is working with the city of Sault Ste. Marie — an Ontario industrial town that’s home to a troubled steel mill — to propose a new port there and develop road and rail infrastructure to better link the resource-rich areas of Canada with domestic consumer markets and trading partners overseas.

The US economy can probably get by with fewer imports from Canada, but such dislocations might get expensive. “I certainly appreciate that the United States could probably survive on less trade with Canada, but I also think that ultimately drives up the costs for everybody,” Hamilton said.
While politicians and trade negotiators squabble, the day-to-day management of the Great Lakes-Seaway system is shared between the governments. Canada controls 13 locks and the US oversees two.

In a speech in late August, Lana Payne, national president of labor group Unifor, credited Canadians with building the seaway, though the major upgrades in the 1950s were a joint effort after Washington’s initial hesitance.

“Canada was feeling really good — it had made a huge contribution to the Second World War and it really felt it was mature,” said Ron Stagg, a retired Toronto Metropolitan University professor and author of a 2010 book on the seaway’s history.

As the engineering plans began to take shape, Canadian officials told the US, “if you don’t want to participate, we’re going to do it ourselves. So the US said, maybe we’ll take part, too,” Stagg said.
Territorial questions have resurfaced. Recently a social media campaign pushed for Canadians to declare sovereignty over the “Strait of Our Moose”.

That’s a reference to the Welland Canal, which sits on the Canadian side of the border and connects Lake Erie with Lake Ontario — it’s how ships get around Niagara Falls. The campaign is also a dig at Trump’s inability so far to restore trade flows through the Strait of Hormuz in the US war with Iran.

Still, the Canadian waterways are unlikely to become weaponized chokepoints during a full-blown trade war: Navigating the St. Lawrence River “shall forever remain free and open for the purposes of commerce to the citizens of the United States,” according to the 1871 Treaty of Washington signed by Great Britain and the US.

Yet tensions do exist in regional shipping, and they go deeper than the recent tariff exchanges between Carney and Trump. US-flagged vessel owners say they’re competing on an unlevel playing field because of rules that favor their Canadian rivals.

Jim Weakley, president of the Lake Carriers’ Association, a Westlake, Ohio-based group representing US shipping companies, declined to comment about the trade dispute, saying it “has not impacted binational maritime trade on the Great Lakes.” That’s partly because most business is conducted in long-term contracts and the spot market is too thin to see any impact, according to Weakley.
A broader issue facing his members has echoes of the Trump administration’s reasons for going after Canada and other trading partners – accusations of unfairness and an openness to China.

“Canada has flagging laws, regulations and practices that endanger the economic viability, efficiency and service reliability of the US-flagged Great Lakes fleet’s binational trade that also has resulted in the shrinking of the US-flagged Great Lakes fleet,” according to a position paper Weakley sent via email.

The disparity “has created a Canadian monopoly on the binational Great Lakes trade,” according to the paper, which lists several grievances, including Canadian support for “the growth of the Chinese shipping building empire and receiving ships that have been subsidized by the Chinese government.”

It’s not that Canadian operators prefer to buy their vessels from China’s producers, said Jason Card, vice president of external affairs with the Chamber of Marine Commerce, a binational group in Ottawa representing ship owners, port operators and other stakeholders.

“It’s difficult to find a shipyard that’s willing to build a laker vessel” because of the unique narrow design and limited orders, said Card, who voiced support for the Trump administration’s efforts to revive American shipbuilding. “There’s not a desire to build far from home, it’s just been the reality for the past several years that there’s no available capacity.”

Card said US carriers have, over the years, largely focused on shipping coal and iron ore through the western lakes with their older and bigger vessels, while the Canadians grew to dominate areas where smaller boats are needed to traverse the locks.
“Unfortunately in the current situation, there’s a pinch on steel, and coal is going out of fashion,” he said.
That’s been a stark reality for local businesses that see ships like American Century as economic workhorses.

At the Duluth port authority, Beardsley notes that Duluth-Superior terminals saw iron ore volumes last year drop by about 3 million tons from a year earlier, mostly because of weaker exports to Canada.

Higher-value breakbulk cargo — like sections of giant wind turbines or industrial machinery — is increasing, though, with the help of an energy sector supplying oil, gas and wind projects spanning the middle of North America.

“We’re hoping that the two countries can come to an understanding and an agreement that’s really mutually beneficial to binational trade,” he said. “That’s the key to success for our port and the region.”

items.title: EU Presses Partners to Deliver Ukraine Funding Ahead of UN Week
body: The European Union is pressing international partners to provide funding to Ukraine as the country faces increasing financing needs amid a tense battlefield situation before the winter.

“When we were putting forward Ukraine support loan, the idea was that should cover around two thirds of Ukraine’s funding needs, and one third should be covered by other international partners,” EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said after a meeting with the bloc’s finance ministers in Dublin, joined by their British, Swiss and Canadian peers.

Earlier this year, the EU adopted a €90 billion ($103 billion) loan package to support Kyiv for 2026-2027, but military costs have already left a shortfall of around $27 billion. The International Monetary Fund, together with the commission, are assessing how substantial Ukraine’s gap will be for next year.

Against this backdrop, the EU is pushing other countries including the UK and Japan to provide financial support and this issue will be on top of EU officials’ agendas when they meet with their counterparts in New York during the United Nations General Assembly next week, people familiar with the matter said.

Ukraine Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko, who also attended the Dublin gathering, said that the 2027 shortfall could be at least $32 billion, but his international partners are still assessing the numbers.
“Ukraine is facing larger funding needs because Russia’s aggression — if anything — is increasing,” Dombrovskis said. “In a relatively short time we should be able to clarify the gap.”

The EU commissioner also acknowledged that discussions for providing financial support would be helped if Ukraine delivers on the reform plan agreed with donors. Some of the proposals, including on taxes, remain stuck in the country’s parliament.

Any progress on reforms and third-country funding support would also help unlock additional money from EU countries, the people added, speaking on condition of anonymity because the discussions are private.

Some EU member states have returned to the idea of using part of €210 billion immobilized Russian central-bank assets in Europe, while others are suggesting that issuing additional joint debt could be the workable solution.

items.title: Bloomberg Green's Pocket Guide to Climate Week NYC 2026
body: New York’s annual climate bazaar is kicking off, and it promises to be as big and hectic as ever. Last year, attendance was estimated at 100,000. If you’re New York-bound, we’ve distilled some of the highlights in a handy mini-agenda, below.

The week’s events run alongside the United Nations General Assembly, and with COP31 approaching, it’s a chance for host Turkey to set the stage for the global talks. But the nation so far isn’t on track to meet the electrification goal it’s trying to rally others around.
Subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to all our coverage.
By Selcan Hacaoglu and Laura Millan

Turkey’s progress on the energy transition is coming under scrutiny as the host of the next UN climate summit tries to rally international support for a new global electrification goal that would require significant policy changes for the country itself to fulfill it.

Ahead of this year’s COP31 climate gathering in Antalya, Turkey is seeking support from policymakers attending Climate Week in New York for a global target of 35% electrification by 2035. The country’s official projections forecast it will only have achieved 25% electrification by that date.

“Very significant policy changes to accelerate renewable electrification would be needed to bring it to 35% by 2035,” said Climate Action Tracker, a non-profit that analyzes countries’ climate goals and their progress in achieving them. “Power generation from wind and solar is increasing, but not enough to displace fossil fuels which are also expanding.”
By Bloomberg News

Climate Week NYC, an annual fixture held alongside the United Nations General Assembly, is back for 2026. The sprawling calendar  includes hundreds of events around the city through Sept. 27 — everything from a morning birdwalk to a sustainable fashion showcase to a compost tour.

Below, our journalists offer a selection of what struck us as intriguing, timely or can’t-miss. One event we’ll give special mention to: Bloomberg Green’s own. Join us on Tuesday and Wednesday for lively conversations with speakers from the World Bank, Amazon, Microsoft, Ben & Jerry’s and more.
Buildings for People, Cities for Life: A New Agenda for Urban Resilience

Instead of treating urban policy and climate policy as separate domains, how can they be fused into a single cohesive agenda? Scheduled speakers at this event, organized by the Danish consulate and partners, include former Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo.
BloombergNEF at Climate Week

For the best-informed insights into what lies ahead, drop by this event featuring a passel of clean economy experts. They’ll talk about global impacts from the Iran war, the outlook for renewables and data centers in the US, the future of advanced transportation and more.
Climate Town & Amy Westervelt Live

Rollie Williams, host of the popular YouTube channel Climate Town, and journalist Amy Westervelt of Drilled Media are teaming up for a ticketed comedy night. Climate disinformation is likely to be one of their targets.
Perspectives Shaping Climate Action Through Sports

Lace up your sneakers and get ready to “plog.” New York Road Runners brings together leaders from the realms of sustainability, science and sports to share their thoughts on meeting the climate challenge. After the panel, participants are invited to head outdoors to collect litter while running or walking. Bags and gloves will be provided.
Climate, Security and America’s Place in a Shifting World

The convergence of energy security and national security demands a rethink of US climate policy. This panel, hosted by the Climate Group, will explore what that means, from scaling technologies to developing leaders and rebuilding coalitions. Scheduled speakers include Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Phil Duffy, chief scientist of Spark Climate Solutions.
Sustainable Investment Forum 2026

This annual, all-day gathering of asset owners and institutional investors will focus on everything from how to shield portfolios from physical risk to governance approaches for artificial intelligence.
Dynamo Energy Transition Summit
An afternoon gathering focused on the future of energy will bring together the tech, banking and energy industries, with representatives of Google, Meta and Bank of America due to speak.
2nd Annual Climate Jam

This benefit concert will raise money for the nonprofit Protect Our Winters, which aims to inspire snowboarders, rock climbers and cross-country runners to take up the climate fight. The evening will feature live music from Karl Denson, saxophonist for the Rolling Stones, and Adam Met of AJR.
Brazil at a Crossroads: From COP30 to the 2026 Elections

Brazil’s elections next month will shape the country’s climate and environmental policies for years to come — with far-reaching consequences for the Amazon and other threatened ecosystems. This event, hosted by Climate Rights International, weighs what’s at stake.
The Future of Data Centers: Technologies to Change the Paradigm

Data centers are at an inflection point, says the MIT Climate Project, and that demands innovation across disciplines and sectors. MIT researchers will present technologies that could reshape the data center in a session that will also convene leaders from technology, infrastructure, capital and policy.
Superpollutant Action Summit
Hosted by Beyond and the We Mean Business Coalition, this daylong event aims to catalyze concrete action on near-term warming agents: methane, black carbon, HFCs and nitrous oxide.
Rethinking Enterprise AI: Where Compute Efficiency Meets Climate Strategy

Representatives of GitHub, Yale and LinkedIn will discuss findings from a new survey of software developers’ climate opinions. Then they’ll discuss how to mobilize IT and sustainability leaders around prioritizing efficiency.
Habitat for Humanity Solar Barnraising

At a co-op on the Lower East Side — the first Habitat for Humanity project that the late President Jimmy Carter worked on — the group’s Solar Collaborative will host a “barnraising” to prepare for the installation of rooftop panels. Be ready to haul some up the stairs.
Building Postcarbon Futures

How do we forge a sustainable future that is both just and resilient? Author Billy Fleming, drawing on his new book that surveys climate justice projects around the world, joins philosopher Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò, sociologist Daniel Aldana Cohen and designer Keller Easterling for a wide-ranging discussion.
The Resilience Test: An Interactive Catastrophic Disaster Simulation

DLA Piper hosts a workshop “that will challenge participants to navigate a realistic, evolving climate scenario,” an exercise intended to yield practical insights into disaster response and risk management.
New Climate Futures

Newlab’s annual gathering returns to the Brooklyn Navy Yard, where more than 1,000 climate tech founders, investors and policymakers will meet and greet. This year’s themes include decarbonizing hard-to-abate industries and strengthening the power grid. The event will also highlight startups working on climate adaptation.
Climate Capital Summit
Some of the biggest firms on Wall Street, from BlackRock to Goldman Sachs and Apollo, will gather with energy and technology executives to discuss scaling finance for climate solutions.
Firebreaks: From Satellites to the Streets

As part of the main Swiss stage at Climate Week, this event hosted by Swissnex and partners considers how advances in remote sensing and Earth observation can help communities adapt to a world in which fire season is longer and more destructive. Following an expert panel, several guests will be invited to pitch their own climate-ready city projects at an open mic.
The Future of the Grid: From Utility Infrastructure to End Users

​Organized by HearstLab, the program will feature live demos from its portfolio companies Buzz Solutions, Symbium and Scope Zero, as well as leaders from government, tech and the utility sector discussing how to build a resilient energy system.
Free Central Park Bike Tour
Unwind after a week of frenetic networking by exploring Central Park on two wheels, courtesy of Holland Bikes.
Nuclear Rooftop Party
Join Nuclear New York and the Nuclear is Clean Energy Club for atomic DJ sets under the stars. 21+.

Working on a short documentary about climate change? Don’t miss your chance to submit it to the Bloomberg Green Docs film competition. Grand prize: $25,000. Submissions will be accepted through October 2, 2026.
See official rules at bloomberg.com/greendocs.

When it comes to green tech, China is a list of superlatives. It produces more solar panels, wind turbines, electric vehicles and batteries than anywhere else in the world. But is finance the real climate hero? This week on Zero, Akshat Rathi is joined by Ma Jun, chairman of the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and former chief economist of China’s central bank. They discuss how the country became a green-finance superpower and how other nations can speed up their own transitions.

items.title: MS NOW Journalists Barred From White House After Trump Ban
body: MS NOW and CNN said its journalists were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday after President Donald Trump said he would bar the cable news networks, along with Politico.
CNN called the move “an illegal assault” on the constitutional rights of news organizations to report without hindrance from government.

An MS NOW reporter, speaking to the network from a street near the White House, said that she and a photographer had their badges confiscated at the gate when they arrived for work, although a producer for the network was allowed to enter.

MS NOW said it will continue to report on the president and his administration. “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalists in our democracy,” the network said in a statement posted on X.
Trump escalated his fight with the media on Friday, citing unfavorable coverage by what he often calls the “fake news.”

Asked by a reporter later Friday in the Oval Office why he decided to ban the outlets now, Trump responded, “It’s really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it.” He also referred to the new policy as “the ban on the free press,” and suggested that he may target other news outlets.

It’s not clear what spurred Trump’s sudden escalation, but it comes at a low water mark for his administration. A wide and unrelenting series of polls have signaled peril for Republicans in upcoming midterm elections, both in the House and the Senate, where seats once considered safe for Republicans are now in play.

Trump continues to be stymied by the war he started with Iran and the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine, both of which are elevating energy prices that weigh on American voters. And Vice President JD Vance has taken to calling on voters not to abandon the party even if they don’t agree with all the administration has done.
The Fed also hiked rates this week, leaving Trump limping into the midterms with mortgages at 7%, diesel fuel above $6 and gasoline above $4.
CNN and Politico on Friday both condemned Trump’s announcement, citing protections under the First Amendment, which bars the government from making laws that abridge freedom of speech and the press.
Trump’s ban is likely to draw a legal challenge. Federal courts have previously overturned the Trump administration’s efforts to bar reporters entirely from the White House campus.
In an earlier spat, the White House excluded the Associated Press from presidential events, though its reporters were still allowed to work from the grounds. The AP sued and the case is ongoing.

During Trump’s first term, the administration revoked press credentials from then-CNN correspondent Jim Acosta after the president and the reporter sparred during a November 2018 news conference. Acosta sued the administration and a federal judge appointed by Trump ordered the press pass restored.

Last year, the White House took control of picking the group of reporters able to cover Trump in smaller environments including Air Force One and the Oval Office. The group, known as the protective pool, had for decades been managed by the White House Correspondents’ Association.
The WHCA, a collection of reporters from news organizations that cover the White House, issued a statement Friday evening supporting the outlets.

“This is about more than the rights of journalists,” WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich said in the statement, adding that the Constitution protects press freedoms whether or not the president likes or approves an organization’s coverage or journalists’ questions. “It is about the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office.”

The move has also drawn pushback even from some conservative figures, who typically abstain from publicly criticizing Trump but say the president would be better served sparring with the press than banning them.

items.title: China Slams US Law Tightening Sanctions on Russia and Iran
body: China criticized the new US law that strengthens sanctions on Russia and extends trade measures on Iran, which was signed late Friday by President Donald Trump.
Bejing has “consistently opposed” unilateral sanctions and so-called secondary sanctions, according to a Commerce Ministry spokesperson.
Specifically, China is against sanctions that lack United Nations authorization or a basis in international law, the spokesperson said in a statement posted on Saturday.
Read more: Trump Signs Russia Sanctions Bill Granting New Tariff Powers

China will closely monitor Washington‘s next steps and reserves the right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty, development interests and the legitimate rights and interests of its companies, while calling for stable trade ties through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said.

Trump on Friday signed a law on Friday a measure authorizing tariffs on countries that buy Russian petroleum products, a move closely watched by Ukraine as it seeks stronger US backing in its war with Russia.
Read more: US, China Trade Teams Set to Huddle in New York on AI, Iran

The top five purchasers of Russian petroleum products — a roster that includes China, India and US allies like Turkey — could be hit with broad new tariffs. Opponents of the bill argue that it could open the door to tariffs on the entire European Union, since some EU member countries continue to buy Russian energy products.

China’s comments come ahead of a high-stakes meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday. Ahead of those talks, US Teasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng will lead talks on trade and other pressure points in New York on Sunday.

items.title: Malaysian Minister to Resign after 1MDB Pardon Sparks Criticism
body: Malaysian Transport Minister Anthony Loke said he plans to resign from cabinet in response to the conditional pardon given to former Prime Minister Najib Razak related to his role in one of the largest corruption scandals in modern history.

“We find it difficult to accept,” Loke said at a press conference Saturday after he and other leaders of the Democratic Action Party — a key pillar of the current Malaysian government — met to discuss its members’ dissatisfaction. “Not just for us, but many Malaysians.”
The announcement is yet another blow to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling coalition, which has been hobbled by poor results in local elections and faces tensions with its government partners.

Last month, DAP held an internal referendum on whether it should remain in government, partly triggered by concerns over how it tackles corruption. Party delegates ultimately voted to stay in government.

Loke said he’ll give Anwar his resignation letter “in the near future” and that other DAP ministers — although also prepared to resign — will remain. A broader round of resignations may force a dissolution of the government, which could benefit the “political ambitions” of other parties, he said.
Read more: Malaysia’s Zahid Seeks Early Polls as UMNO Plots Return to Power

Loke’s decision came the day after Malaysian King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar allowed Najib to serve out the remainder of a prison term under house arrest. The reprieve drew widespread condemnation from civil society groups, politicians and voters, with some questioning the government’s commitment to combating graft.

Najib, 73, was originally sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined 210 million ringgit ($51 million) in one of the cases brought against him related to the 1MDB scandal. Two years ago, then-King Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah halved the sentence and cut his fine to 50 million ringgit.

The Federal Territories Pardons Board is chaired by the sitting king. It also includes Attorney-General of Malaysia Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar, cabinet minister Hannah Yeoh, and three other members appointed by the king.

In 2025 Najib was convicted in another 1MDB-related corruption case, sentenced to 15 years in prison, and assessed a 11.4 billion ringgit fine. He has appealed the verdict. This week’s royal intervention doesn’t cover that conviction.

items.title: ECB Must Be 'Vigilant' But Not Rush Action, Stournaras Says
body: The European Central Bank must be mindful of upside inflation risks but shouldn’t act hastily, according to Governing Council member Yannis Stournaras.

While it’s “good news” that there are so far no second-round effects via things like wages, it can’t be taken for granted that the situation will persist, the Greek central-bank chief said in an interview.

“We are seeing a continuum of supply-side shocks and we cannot simply look through that, and at the same time, there’s also a strong demand element due to fiscal expansion and the boom in AI Investment,” he said in Dublin, where he’s attending a meeting of European finance ministers and central bankers. “We must remain vigilant.”

Policymakers, who’ve raised borrowing costs twice since the Iran war broke out, are debating what more they need to do to return inflation to 2% from more than 3% now. Some say the surprisingly robust performance of the region’s economy gives them leeway to hike further. Others, though, worry that growth can’t withstand much more tightening.
With more than a month until the next decision, Stournaras signaled he hasn’t made up his mind, and that the various economic outlooks prepared by the ECB may serve as a guide.

“If there’s an inflation surge in September or a rise in energy costs that take us well into the adverse scenario, a hike in October can’t be excluded,” he said. “But if there is a bit of doubt, we’ll not do anything and wait until the next round of forecasts. There’s no need to rush action.”

As oil and natural gas prices rise once again, President Christine Lagarde stressed that upswings in energy markets don’t necessarily translate into higher interest rates. Even so, other Governing Council members speaking to Bloomberg in the Irish capital prepared the ground for further moves.

Markets are leaning toward a third quarter-point increase in the deposit rate next month, to 2.75%. After that, they see at least two more before inflation is dealt with, though economists are less sure policy will require that level of tightening.
Stournaras cautioned that the backdrop remains volatile.

“If data on the economy shows that resilience doesn’t continue or activity growth is decelerating, I think that would be a reason not to hike, and a reason to pause,” he said. Also, “if there’s an agreement in the Middle East, it could bring energy prices down very quickly again.”

Stournaras stressed that this week’s hike by the Federal Reserve also helps the ECB. “The Fed’s rate decision was positive for its credibility and for the credibility of monetary policy worldwide, because of the central role played by the Fed and the dollar.”

The debate about the ECB’s next steps is happening against a backdrop of rising bond yields in the euro zone, with a measure of French risk on Friday exceeding one percentage point for the first time in 14 years amid growing caution among investors over the country’s wide budget deficit and political uncertainty.
For Stournaras, the situation is still under control, though he added that political developments will play an important role in how it evolves.

“Up to now at least, we haven’t seen any big turmoil,” he said. “I hope governments continue to be aware of the need to be fiscally prudent given our past experience with policies that aren’t careful enough.”

items.title: China Starts Campaign to Combat Environmental Monitoring Fraud
body: China outlined a nationwide effort to target false reporting by environmental monitoring institutions at a meeting attended by multiple government agencies, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment said in a statement on its WeChat account.
Autorities in Beijing have for over a decade raised concerns about the quality of the monitoring of and reporting on pollutants released by chemical producers, the energy industry, and others.
Environment Minister Huang Runqiu on Saturday said falsification remains a serious problem despite efforts to strengthen oversight and combat fraud.

Huang called for stronger inspections and spot checks, enhanced cross-source data comparison and intelligent screening capabilities, and closer coordination among authorities, including those responsible for environmental, market regulation, public security, prosecutorial and judicial activities.
He also said suspected criminal cases should be transferred promptly in accordance with the law.

items.title: Practical Magic 2 Is a Gamble on the Power of Cult Movies
body: To kick off the fall box office swing, Practical Magic 2 summoned $30 million domestically over its opening weekend. It’s a solid if unspectacular start for a film with a $75 million production budget, but what’s most surprising is that the sequel was greenlit to begin with. The original Practical Magic, released in 1998, didn’t have the commercial performance (or positive critical sentiment) that would typically warrant a follow-up. Instead, the film developed a cult following over the years that appreciated its witchy depiction of sisterhood.

Practical Magic 2’s existence is one example of how Hollywood is using cult-movie sequels to expand its definition of viable IP. If these movies have a devoted following, the thinking goes, then that enthusiasm can translate into stronger ticket sales for the sequel.

Except that’s not exactly a foolproof calculation. Cultural staying power and commercial success aren’t necessarily interchangeable for cult movies. Treating them as such can leave studios vulnerable to mistaking a passionate audience for a sufficiently large one.These sort of movies are easy to recognize but tricky to define in broad terms. Generally, they struggle at the box office and are initially rejected by critics. A film’s reclamation can be achieved through home video releases, cable reruns, midnight screenings, and critical reappraisals. Thanks to video-on-demand and streaming services, the distance between a film’s rejection by the mainstream and its second life as a cult classic has also narrowed. The Empty Man, for instance, was unceremoniously released by 20th Century Studios at the height of the pandemic before a cult following emerged from its VOD release.

For studios, a film’s box office performance is one of the most reliable barometers for whether it merits a sequel. But the fanbases behind cult movies can alter the perception of these projects from curious misfires into dormant IP with untapped commercial potential.

As a result, studios aren’t just weighing whether to greenlight a sequel, but what kind of budget that enthusiasm can realistically justify. Consider Blade Runner. Despite an underwhelming release in 1982 — the film had the misfortune of coming out in the same month as E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial — Ridley Scott’s sci-fi neo-noir was later celebrated as one of the high points in the genre. With decades of goodwill, a sequel in 2017 seemed like a worthy bet.

Blade Runner 2049 cost $185 million, compared with the original’s $30 million budget, which was equivalent to about $76 million in 2017. Despite overwhelming critical acclaim and a pair of Oscar wins, however, the sequel still fell short of its reported $400 million break-even point. The franchise was effectively treated as blockbuster IP when its commercial ceiling was closer to that of a niche genre property.

When larger budgets aren’t matched by commensurate box office returns, one viable alternative is taking a sequel straight to streaming. This is what Disney opted to do with Hocus Pocus 2, which landed exclusively on Disney+ in 2022. It set a Nielsen streaming movie record with 2.7 billion minutes of viewing in its opening weekend. A third film is in development — though, as Variety notes, its streaming success has the studio mulling a theatrical rollout.
Perhaps Disney should consider the fate of another ‘90s cult classic centered on witches before making the final call.

First, the good: Practical Magic 2’s opening weekend is hardly a disaster, and it has a couple of factors working in its favor for a sustained run. Having returning stars like Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock, who remain meaningful box office draws, is certainly helpful. According to Deadline, Practical Magic 2 also tapped into a specific demographic of moviegoers. Nearly 80% of its opening weekend audience was female and 36% were over the age of 45, suggesting it’s reaching the demographic that helped make it a cult hit in the first place.

Now for the not so good: There’s little evidence so far that the franchise’s commercial bona fides have improved over time. The sequel’s $30 million domestic debut is comparable, when adjusted for inflation, to the original film’s $13.1 million opening weekend. But to merely match the first film’s $94.4 million worldwide gross in inflation-adjusted terms, the sequel needs to make roughly $194 million. That’s a lot of ground to cover.

The sequel at least had a more conservative budget. Practical Magic 2’s reported $75 million production cost is nominally the same as the original film’s, but the sequel represents a smaller investment in today’s dollars. Still, nearly three decades of cult status haven’t yet translated into obvious commercial growth, leaving the sequel’s upside uncertain.

Not every cult sequel is destined to fail or to be only suitable for streaming. The Riddick franchise shows how to approach that risk sensibly. After the original film, 2000’s Pitch Black, became a modest theatrical hit and a DVD phenomenon — selling more than 2 million copies — Vin Diesel reprised his role in 2004’s The Chronicles of Riddick. It underperformed against its nine-figure production budget. But instead of cutting its losses, Universal Pictures returned to the character with 2013’s Riddick, which cost $38 million (far less than its predecessor, even after adjusted for inflation) and grossed nearly $100 million worldwide.
The smaller scale made Riddick a considerably less risky theatrical proposition. How responsibly a cult sequel is budgeted can be just as important as understanding the size of its audience.

All told, there is no magic bullet for studios to determine when — or if — a movie crosses the threshold from niche property to viable franchise. Cult status can tell Hollywood that an audience still cares about a movie. It can’t always conjure the box office to match.

items.title: AI's Threats Demand a Better Movie Analogy Than The Terminator
body: As fear of what unfettered AI could mean for humanity has exploded into the public consciousness, media commentators have been grasping for ways to help understand what that really means. Not surprisingly, many found points of reference in movies, with The Terminator’s Skynet becoming “self-aware” as shorthand for conceptualizing how “tech run amok” could trigger our demise.

The problem with the killer AI genre, alas, is that it becomes a bit convoluted. The Terminator detoured into time travel. The Matrix explored an alternate reality and became incomprehensible in the sequels. Everyone who saw 2001: A Space Odyssey surely remembers the HAL-9000 computer going rogue, but in adapting Arthur C. Clarke’s book, the film wasn’t completely explicit as to why.

That’s why those using pop culture references to convey what’s at stake should consider evoking a different genre — namely, the 1950s monster movies from the early days of the Cold War and the nuclear age. Their more straightforward cause-and-effect plots offer a better analogy for the damage AI has already shown it can do: Children have died by suicide after talking to chatbots, people are losing their jobs to the technology and data centers are seen as an environmental threat.

The wedding of AI and doomsday scenarios has already prompted multiple warnings, but the alarm bells entered a new phase thanks to former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon. In a Wall Street Journal interview and viral social media thread, he outlined how companies like Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s posts were alarming enough, racking up millions of views, but others in the field concurred, suggesting these weren’t the ravings of some wild-eyed lunatic but ought to serve as a call to action.

The question becomes how to help laypeople get their heads around a topic that sounds like the stuff of science fiction. While there are plenty of pop culture examples warning about artificial intelligence — dating back to the 1970s — framing the discussion in a less wonky manner, against the backdrop of nuclear Armageddon and radiation, feels more germane.

The monster films were rife with what entertainment publication Collider called “atomic anxiety,” as nuclear blasts awakened ancient beasts and transformed the mundane into existential threats. Think The Beast from 20,000 Fathoms and Godzilla, which had particular resonance with a Japanese audience that witnessed the horrors of the atomic bomb firsthand. Those monsters were joined by a wave of irradiated giant bugs, including Them! (ants), Beginning of the End (locusts), and Tarantula.

While the idea of scientists meddling with uncontrollable forces was nothing new — consider literary staples such as Frankenstein and Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde — the atomic age cast those stories in another (and much bigger) light as a means of thrilling audiences. Tarantula, for example, featured a scientist experimenting with a “super-nutrient” intended to eradicate world hunger, only to turn loose a rampaging 100-foot-tall creature.

In an academic sense, one early AI movie, Colossus: The Forbin Project, might provide the clearest intellectual road map for the damage the technology can unleash. The chilling story, which was probably years ahead of its time, involved a computer superintelligence intended to oversee America’s nuclear arsenal that begins communicating with its Soviet counterpart and conspires to take over the world. The monster movies, however, are more visceral, which might be necessary to awaken a public, as medical and biosecurity expert Ashish Jha recently tweeted, that’s “sleepwalking into a potentially huge disaster.”

History suggests that the right cinematic framing can make an abstract existential threat feel immediate. The image of mad scientists losing control over their creations in the ’50s has been very useful. As Tom Nichols wrote in The Atlantic in 2025, Hollywood gave us the language to process the prospect of nuclear catastrophe. He noted that when he taught undergraduates born after the Cold War ended, the notion of such annihilation “seemed mysterious, and even irrelevant. … And then it occurred to me: They haven’t seen the movies.”

Given the dire nature of the latest warnings, this doesn’t feel like the time for subtlety. And while The Terminator and The Matrix gave physical form to the threatSmaller-boned fares like 2014's Ex Machina deserve honorable mention. , the monster metaphor — and the way those movies reflected the anxiety of that moment — seems like as good a way as any to help process the conversation.

After Coxon’s posts, the discourse and urgency did seem to abruptly shift, with even our modern mad scientists recognizing they might have a problem. Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei wrote an essay in which he proposed slowing down the AI industry, and OpenAI’s Sam Altman quickly followed suit. Whether those prudent-sounding steps represent a true awakening or a shrewd public-relations stunt remains to be seen. The Trump administration’s opposition to AI guardrails, however, indicates a partisan divide that doesn’t bode well for meaningful action, at least for now.

If we can hit the brakes in time on AI, perhaps we’ll be able to look back at this period the way we do when viewing those old black-and-white movies, amused that fake-looking giant bugs ever scared us. Then again, it would frankly be reassuring, based on recent headlines, just to know we’ll be here to look back at all.

items.title: Hyrox Incident Shows Dangers of Letting Ambition Outrun Growth
body: This is the Weekend Edition of Bloomberg Opinion Today, a roundup of the most popular stories Bloomberg Opinion publishes each week based on web readership. New subscribers can sign up here; follow us on Bluesky, TikTok, Instagram, LinkedIn and Threads.

Hyrox takes its sporting credentials seriously — it was, after all, co-founded by an Olympian. But the commercial success of the high-endurance fitness race isn’t built on the backs of elite athletes. It comes from attracting overachieving gym junkies.

Which is why the competition must now make amends to its core group of devotees after mishandling a hygiene controversy in Beijing over the weekend, especially as it sets its sights on becoming an even bigger force in global fitness. The women’s world record holder, Australia’s Joanna Wietrzyk, was allowed to complete (and win) despite experiencing bowel incontinence partway through the race.

The viral episode caused an uproar among participants upset about the prospect of having to share dirty equipment, a reaction that quickly reverberated through the international community. There was also the issue of fairness. Existing rules penalize behaviors that can affect the cleanliness and safety of communal spaces, such as spitting. Allowing a competitor to continue after soiling herself struck many as a glaring inconsistency.

items.title: Midterm Voting Starts in Key States With Election 45 Days Out
body: It’s 45 days before an Election Day that will determine control of Congress for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s second term and 20 states are already mailing ballots to voters. That includes the hard-fought Senate contests in Texas, Michigan and North Carolina.

Tens of millions of Americans will have already cast their ballots before Nov. 3, thanks largely to the Supreme Court earlier this week blocking an effort by the Trump administration to add new restrictions to voting by mail. Thirteen states will in the next 15 days join those that have already sent ballots to voters.

Meanwhile, early in-person voting started Friday in Idaho, Minnesota, South Dakota and Virginia, according to the Center for Election Innovation and Research, marking the final stretch of an election season that has increasingly become a referendum on Trump.

All of this voting gets underway amid weeks of bruising economic news for Republicans, including an uptick in gasoline and diesel prices, stubborn inflation, increases in mortgage rates and drops in consumer sentiment. But House Speaker Mike Johnson insisted this week that Republicans aren’t nervous that voter dissatisfaction with the economy will hurt them at the polls.

“We’re constantly coming up with new and innovative things to continue to work to bring down the cost of living,” he told reporters Wednesday after sending lawmakers home earlier than scheduled until after the election.
Read More: Midterm Battlegrounds Hit by Diesel, Heating Oil Price Spikes

Still, just over a week after the Republican midterm convention, the two-day bonanza hasn’t yielded the bump in polls that often follows political conventions. Democrats lead Republicans by nearly nine percentage points on a generic ballot, according to averages compiled by Real Clear Politics.

“Let’s be clear about one thing: Democrats now have the advantage on every issue,” House Majority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Thursday, pointing to favorable polling on the economy, healthcare and the war in Iran. “The public is with us.”
Trump at times has seemed resigned to losing GOP control of Congress even as he has sought to tilt the race in Republicans’ favor with mixed results.

His push for a mid-decade redrawing of House districts created a slight advantage for Republicans. But his effort to restrict mail-in ballots was rejected by the Supreme Court, which halted a US Postal Service rule requiring states to adopt uniform envelopes for ballots and submit a list of eligible voters to an online portal.
Read more: Democrats See Wider Path to Take Senate as Trump Backlash Grows

Linda Farmer, auditor for Pierce County, Washington., said that officials are “breathing a huge sigh of relief” after the Supreme Court’s decision. Washington, which will send ballots out next month, exclusively conducts elections by mail.

“We’ve been busy trying to get the word out that your ballots will come to you,” Farmer told reporters at a briefing hosted by Partnership for Large Election Jurisdictions. She added that they’re also urging voters to return their ballots early or to use drop boxes to avoid any problems due to postal delays, especially in rural areas.

Trump, who has voted by mail, has long railed against the practice and vowed to do away with mail-in ballots entirely, despite little evidence of fraud. The practice has grown more popular, surging during the pandemic. In the 2024 presidential election, nearly a third of votes were cast by mail. In eight states and Washington, D.C., all voters receive ballots in the mail.

items.title: France Says 2027 Budget Plan Respects EU Spending Guidelines
body: France’s government said its draft 2027 budget bill will meet the European Union’s recommendations on spending as it seeks to reassure financial markets after missing this year’s deficit target.

The Budget Ministry said in a statement Saturday that its plan foresees a 0.7% increase in net primary expenditure in 2027, while the European Commission’s recommendation is for a rise of no more than 1.2%.

France is straining to get a grip on public finances amid weak growth and rising interest costs. On Thursday, the government announced it’s veered off course this year and the deficit will rise to 5.4% instead of narrowing slightly to 5% as set out in the finance law.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said he’ll propose a €54 billion ($62 billion) “effort” to curb the trend increase in outlays and meet the 5% objective in 2027.

But it’s uncertain whether France’s minority government will be able to get its latest finance bill through parliament, where opposition lawmakers are reluctant to compromise before presidential elections. It is due to submit full proposals to lawmakers at the end of September.

The political and fiscal uncertainty has added to selling pressures on global bond markets, pushing up France’s borrowing costs further than other European countries. On Friday, the the yield premium on French 10-year bonds over Germany rose through 100 basis points for the first time in 14 years.

Speaking after a meeting of financial officials in Dublin, EU Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said his department will formally assess budget plans in November, adding that the rise in French yields reflects global market moves.

“France is part of a broader trend which is also in other countries,” Dombrovskis said. “But at the same time, and as we discussed yesterday, it reinforces the message for member states, especially high-debt member states, performing prudent fiscal policies and also meeting their fiscal targets.”
France’s credit rating was downgraded by Scope Ratings on Friday and Morningstar DBRS shifted its outlook to negative.

“Fiscal dynamics have continued to deteriorate reflecting repeated fiscal slippage and the government’s difficulties in meeting self-imposed deficit targets,” Scope said. “The sharp rise in government bond yields since January 2026 will further increase borrowing costs, further constraining fiscal flexibility and increasing the scale of the adjustment required to stabilize public debt.”

The draft finance bill sent to France’s public finances watchdog targets a reduction in spending as a share of economic output to 56.9% in 2027 from 57.1% in 2026, the Budget Ministry said. On the same basis, tax revenues would be 44.2%.
According to the plan, France’s debt ratio would rise to 121.7% of economic output in 2027 from 119.3% this year and 115.7% in 2025.

items.title: A Concrete Case for the Most Beautiful Architecture in the World
body: Welcome back to Pursuits Weekly! This week, Annika Inampudi joins me to look at the world’s biggest culture stories, as well as ideas and recommendations around travel, dining and art. Sign up here to get this newsletter every Saturday in your inbox.
Concrete gets a bad rap, not least in a new documentary, The History of Concrete, which I wrote about this week. It cracks, it erodes, it’s generally considered unsightly.

The director, John Wilson, worries about water leaking through the concrete floor of his basement and witnesses the disintegration of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway. He interviews a woman who drops out of an endurance race because the concrete she’s running on was too unforgiving. He also casts a skeptical eye on the pro-construction agenda of former New York City Mayor Eric Adams.

But concrete is not always ugly or annoying. Every country in the world boasts stunning concrete structures, which are well worth seeking out in your travels but that are all too often overlooked. Visitors to Rome will go see the Pantheon, the nearly 2,000-year-old masterpiece of concrete construction. They’re much less likely to journey three miles north to the Palazzetto dello Sport, the gorgeous 1957 homage by Pier Luigi Nervi, built in just 40 days out of prefabricated panels.

Often travelers will encounter fantastic concrete architecture just because they happen to be staying there. They might have checked in to Eero Saarinen’s TWA Hotel in New York, perhaps, or the Sheraton Grand Doha. Very few, however, will be lucky enough to spend the night at Moshe Safdie’s rectilinear Habitat 67, in Montreal, or Francisco Javier Sáenz de Oiza’s circles-based Torres Blancas in Madrid.

Many of the most beautiful concrete buildings are churches, starting with the Antoniuskirche in Basel, Switzerland, Karl Moser’s 1925 masterpiece. About 50 miles to the west is Le Corbusier’s unsurpassable 1955 Notre-Dame du Haut, in Ronchamp, France. Further north, in Germany, one can find Gottfried Bohm’s multilayered Pilgrimage Church in Neviges, from 1968, and Peter Zumthor’s stripped-down and roofless Bruder Klaus Field Chapel, in Mechernich, from 2007.

On the outskirts of Vienna, seek out Fritz Wotruba’s Wotrubakirche, built in 1976 from 152 concrete blocks of different sizes. Get on a plane, and you can visit Félix Candela’s 1955 Iglesia de la Medalla Milagrosa in Mexico City, or Oscar Niemeyer’s 1960 Cathedral of Brasilia or Tadao Ando’s 1989 Church of Light in Osaka, Japan.

There’s plenty of secular architecture too. The Hoover Dam in Nevada! The Salginatobel Bridge in Switzerland! The National Theatre in London! Alejandro Aravena’s innovation center in Santiago de Chile! The Metro in Washington, DC!

Sometimes, as with La Pyramide, a crumbling shopping mall in Ivory Coast or many of the Yugoslav Spomeniks, antifascist monuments dating to the Tito regime, the concrete is indeed falling apart. But often it’s still pristine and lovely, as with Ryue Nishizawa’s ethereal Teshima Art Museum in Japan. Visit just a few of these structures and you might start feeling a lot more well-disposed towards this often disliked material.

In a time of lots of existential questions, some people are thinking smaller. Madison Darbyshire spent a week at miniatures school, where even the Barbie doll is too big. Fueled by viral social media posts and a desire to go analog, the miniatures community has seen a surge of interest in recent years. The hobby tends to grow popular in times of rapid technological advancement, as people turn to “endangered” crafts as a way to slow down.

While modern Japan can be known for its minimalist decor and open interiors, a new guard of entrepreneurs is revisiting the country’s maximalist past, writes Brandon Presser. Amid a weak yen and economic uncertainty, the popularity of the mid-20th century “Showa retro” aesthetic represents a nostalgia-ridden return to a more analog time, which prized human connection and uniqueness over the great blanding and isolating sameness of modern design.

As a generation of American boomers start to pass down their carefully curated art collections that their heirs may not want, another collecting cohort is growing rapidly across the world. India’s nouveau riche have supercharged its nascent market at home and abroad, James Tarmy and Menaka Doshi report. “The wealthier people in India have finally accepted the fact that the best legacy they can leave behind is art and culture,” says auctioneer Dinesh Vazirani.

Amid a widespread “fun shortage,” this summer represented the return of joyous social moments, from Love Island USA watch parties to a historic Knicks run to World Cup revelry. But don’t dread winter’s cabin fever just yet! Some cities are trying to keep the fun alive, enacting policies relaxing restrictive liquor laws and promoting social vibrancy, Annika Inampudi reports.
“Wow you got a lot of sun this summer” is not a compliment no matter how you mean it. But even I will concede that right now, my skin looks too tired and splotchy.

So in August I tested out La Prairie’s White Caviar Light Infusion Essence ($370), an easily absorbed liquid used after cleansing that smooths out your skin, reduces dull spots and brightens things generally. It was fine. As a person with freckles, which are concentrations of melanin, uniform is not my goal, but it did smooth things a bit. (No matter how often laser dermatologists and plastic surgeons offer to remove them, my freckles are my face — and I think if they totally went away, it would freak out my family and friends. Plus, I like them.)

For the (luxury) price, I found the brand’s White Caviar Light Infusion eye serum ($445) much more worth it. Thickening niacinamide, “micronutrients” from actual caviar (sure), and light pigment molecules helped hollow dark circles. It also, in my testing, reduced fine lines. Which after a season of fun made hearing “You’ve still got a little nice color!” a compliment that I can live with. —Chris Rovzar

items.title: World Running Short of Supertankers Threatens Long-Haul Oil Flow
body: The soaring cost of moving oil around the world is making some long-distance crude trades uneconomical, threatening to disrupt flows at a time when fuel markets have never been tighter.

The jump is being driven by a shortage of available supertankers. In some parts of the world, there are barely any of the ships — each the length of three football fields — left for hire. The squeeze is making faraway barrels less attractive and encouraging refiners to snap up supplies closer to home if they can find them.

Moving a cargo from Houston to Asia now adds about $26 a barrel — $52 million a cargo — to the cost of supplying the world’s largest crude-importing region. That’s equal to roughly a quarter of the price of West Texas Intermediate futures. Before the war, shipping typically accounted for only a tiny fraction of the cost.

The rally is minting fortunes for the small group of shipowners that dominate the tanker market — several industry executives and brokers said the surge would previously have been unimaginable. The value of the world’s largest oil tanker equities soared to a record of almost $70 billion this week.

But for oil traders, the risk is that shipping becoming prohibitively expensive. They’re concerned that the higher costs make it unprofitable for some refiners to turn crude into fuels, deterring them from buying cargoes that have to sail over long distances, even when demand to make diesel and gasoline is strong.

On the industry’s main benchmark route, very large crude carriers hauling 2 million barrels of crude from the Persian Gulf to China are earning upward of $1.2 million a day. Similar pressures are now spreading across the freight market globally.

“It has never been this expensive to move oil around,” Saad Rahim, chief economist at trading giant Trafigura Group, said at the Bloomberg Commodity Investor Forum on Thursday. With freight becoming a larger portion of the value of the cargo, “it becomes a much bigger issue now when you start to think of that in terms of logistics.”
Some long-haul routes that became crucial after wars disrupted energy flows are now looking unattractive as a result of the surge.

Ship-tracking data from Vortexa show US-Asia flows have fallen in recent weeks, as freight costs roughly tripled. A Japanese refiner recently bought a cargo of Alaskan crude — a grade not typically well-suited for the country’s processors — because of the relatively short sailing distance, people familiar with the matter said.
In contrast, the clamor for nearby barrels shows up in Europe’s crude prices.

While Brent futures topped out close to $110 a barrel this week, the European Dated Brent physical crude price climbed above $131 as buyers hunted short-haul cargoes. The region’s processors are also scrambling to replace barrels from the Middle East after Saudi Arabia gave no cargoes to European buyers under their term contracts for next month.
Further afield, sales of Angolan oil, which usually sails thousands of miles to buyers in China, are sluggish.

“Current freight levels can become self-limiting over time — they eventually close arbitrage routes and reduce demand for the most expensive long-haul barrels,” said Sumit Ritolia, senior manager of modeling at analytics firm Kpler.

Shipbrokers with years of experience said they’ve never seen supertanker availability so tight, while multiple industry executives said they’ve never known a market like it. Many said there are few, if any, of the vessels available for hire in certain locations, depending on the timeframe in which they are required.
That’s rippling down to smaller ships.

Asian refiners are turning to 700,000-barrel Aframax tankers for some purchases from the US, rather than the supertankers typically used for those journeys. Shipments loading from ports in the Atlantic, including Brazil, are being booked on two 1 million-barrel Suezmax vessels rather one supertanker with twice that capacity, traders and shipbrokers said.
It’s dragged earnings for smaller vessels higher too. Earnings for Suezmaxes are on average north of $300,000 a day, rates typically associated with sailing in and out of war zones.

The biggest drivers of the surge are twofold: the knock-on effects of the US-Iran conflict, and a huge wager by a South Korean tycoon that was already sending shipping rates higher before the war began.

Vessels shuttling barrels through the Strait of Hormuz are sucking up more ships for longer as they switch cargoes near Oman. Other tankers are sailing thousands of miles around Africa to pick up cargoes in the Mediterranean, while until now, Asian buyers swapped lost Middle Eastern barrels for longer-haul supplies from the Americas. Those factors all help stretch out the tanker fleet and boost rates.

The key for oil traders is how long elevated freight rates can be sustained. Diesel futures in Europe are near $200 a barrel, a sign the region’s processors still need to get their hands on every cargo they can.

“Freight has never taken a big part of the delivered cost of oil, but it’s now playing a much bigger role in oil markets,” said Xavier Tang, senior market analyst at analytics firm Vortexa. “This is having a knock-on effect on end buyers.”

items.title: US, China Trade Teams Set to Huddle in New York on AI, Iran
body: Supply Lines is a daily newsletter that tracks global trade. Sign up here.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng will lead talks on trade and other pressure points Sunday in New York ahead of next week’s summit between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.

The negotiators will lay the groundwork for a high-profile meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept. 24 in Washington. Bessent and He last met face-to-face near Seoul four months ago, just days before Trump visited Beijing in May.

Energy disruptions from the Iran war, the artificial intelligence boom, and trade and investment are likely to top the agenda as both sides work to maintain stability in a tariff truce that expires in November. Adding urgency for US officials to extend the deal are Nov. 3 midterm elections where inflation is a persistent voter concern.

The US is “at a stage with China where efforts to try and transform this relationship and strengthen it are no longer top of list,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
The objective is more about “trying to keep things stable, keep things from escalating and try to, in practical terms, keep the trade truce that was reached in Busan in place,” she said.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will also attend talks, according to a statement from his office.

“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue balanced trade with China by monitoring the implementation of recent commitments, optimizing trade in non-sensitive goods, and improving market access for American farmers, manufacturers, and workers,” he said in the statement late Friday.
An announcement of new US tariffs over allegations of trading partners’ excess manufacturing capacity has been delayed until after the meeting, according to people familiar with the matter.

“Both sides want to avoid another flare-up and relative stability in the relationship is likely to continue,” Nicole Gorton-Caratelli, Adam Farrar and Maeva Cousin of Bloomberg Economics wrote in a research note this week. “But as the US rebuilds its tariff wall, the risk of renewed escalation remains.”

The US and China have been working to reduce levies on American energy and agricultural products, Bloomberg reported earlier, part of a broader initiative to ease barriers on $30 billion worth of products from each side under the Board of Trade mechanism launched earlier this year.
Chinese exports to the US have rebounded this year, showing the limits of Trump’s tariffs but also reflecting a surge in demand for AI-related electronics produced by China.
The New York talks are taking place ahead of the United Nations General Assembly meeting held in the city later next week.

Bessent and He have held a series of discussion over the past 18 months mostly in a third country to portray a sense of neutrality. Whether the meeting in New York signals greater trust or merely convenience given the UN meeting, it also suggests the next round will be in China for the sake of reciprocity.

Bloomberg reported earlier this week that Chinese officials were considering BYD Co. for a possible business delegation joining Xi at the summit — a potentially provocative move given Trump’s tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles.
Trump has suggested he might be willing to allow a Chinese car company to build in the US, if it did so with American workers.
One Chinese official familiar with planning for the meeting said China’s top issue would be Taiwan, particularly a planned US weapons sale.

Easier discussions will be held around tariffs and agricultural products like soybeans, while AI, autos, technology and e-commerce will feature on the agenda, said the official, who asked for anonymity to discuss private conversations. The official added that China would offer more permits for rare earths as a bargaining chip, without disclosing details on what Beijing would seek in return.

Maintaining flows of Chinese rare-earth magnets was a priority for Trump when he agreed last year’s truce. Since then, China’s monthly exports of the critical industrial components have been running substantially below the levels that prevailed before Beijing imposed export controls in April 2025.
In recent weeks, AI has rapidly emerged as a new fault line between the US and China.
Washington has restricted China’s access to advanced chips and accused Chinese firms of developing their own domestic models by “distilling” capabilities from American tech.

Beijing has pushed back on calls from US tech leaders to pace AI development in the interest of safety, with the country’s foreign ministry dismissing such moves as “fear-mongering” and state media denouncing them as “self-serving.”
“As the number one and number two superpowers in AI by a lot, it behooves all of us to put up guardrails, to have close communication,” Bessent told reporters earlier this month.
In a statement to Axios this week, the Treasury secretary said “we are open to discussions on avoiding shared risks and avoiding bifurcation of our two systems.”
The US moves, Beijing says, are designed to contain its rise, and China refuses to let Washington take the lead on writing the rules for AI.

A more immediate threat to both economies is the energy shock, and the White House has stepped up pressure on Iran and its trading partners. China provides Tehran with an economic lifeline as the biggest buyer of Iranian oil.

Bessent’s Treasury Department is ratcheting up pressure on financial institutions as part of its effort to choke off trade and financial flows between Iran and rest of the world, fueling speculation that Chinese banks could be targeted.

Bessent said during testimony to the House Financial Services Committee earlier this week that he’s had “private discussions” with Chinese officials on the issue and hoped to make further progress during the upcoming talks this weekend.

A US naval blockade has sharply curtailed crude oil flows to China, raising the prospect of refinery run cuts in the coming weeks across the teapot sector, which makes up one-third of national refining capacity.

“China has an interest in reopening Hormuz, but limited leverage to force either side to change course,” said Jesse Marks, founder of Rihla Research & Advisory and former Middle East policy adviser in the US government. “The longer the Strait remains closed, the more US sanctions and the wider disruption to regional trade will begin to cut into China’s own economic interests in Iran.”
